title: Transparency Statements That Diffuse Distrust During Moments of Genuine Connection e-connection-mgcs
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart draws on research about police-community interactions to propose a concrete refinement to the MGC (Moments of Genuine Connection) practice: transparency statements at the very opening of each teacher-student micro-interaction. Research found that the first 45 words of a police-civilian encounter significantly predicted the quality of the entire interaction, with transparency statements—explaining the reason for the approach—dramatically improving tone and trust. Stuart applies this directly to classroom MGCs, providing a sample script and outlining the four research-identified criteria for effective transparency statements: early timing, benevolent intent, genuine authenticity, and personal first-person framing rather than institutional language. The piece is a focused, practical upgrade to an existing strategy rather than a new idea.
points: The first 45 words of a teacher-student MGC set the tone for the entire interaction, making a brief, honest opening statement of purpose an unusually high-leverage investment in the quality of each micro-moment.

A transparency statement for an MGC briefly explains why the teacher is pulling the student aside—‘I’m working through students this week to get to know each of you better so I can give you a good experience this year’—which signals positive intent before the student can form a defensive interpretation.

Four criteria make transparency statements effective: timing (first thing said), conveyed benevolence (honest positive rationale), genuine authenticity, and first-person personal framing rather than institutional or policy-referencing language.

The research validates what the MGC framework already aims for—authentic, individually addressed care signals—but provides a structural opening script that is especially useful with students who approach teacher attention with suspicion or defensiveness.
quotes: these brief (30- to 90-second) encounters with students can often be awkward and sometimes even threatening to students.
Researchers found that the first 45 words in an encounter between a community member and a police officer were highly predictive of the tenor and quality of the whole encounter.

Hi, Destiny, how’s it going? I’m pulling students aside this week, just trying to get to know each of you better so I can give you a good experience this year. Is it okay if I talk to you for a minute?
Timing: The statement comes right at the beginning, setting the tone for the interaction. Benevolence: Conveying an honest, positive rationale for the interaction.
Genuine: Obviously, I can’t agree with this one more, given that MGCs are meant to be real, authentic signals to students that we value, know, and respect them.
Personal and addressing the situation at hand, in the first person: “I want to be a good teacher for you.” Versus institutional, “Our school has a new initiative to get to know students.
